stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a survey of 140 highway bridges, engineers found that decks treated with a silane sealant showed roughly half as much surface cracking after fifteen years as untreated decks. The team concluded that the sealant substantially slows deck deterioration and recommended applying it statewide.

Text 2
The survey's crack counts are not in question. However, the sealed decks were mostly built after 2005, under stricter concrete-mix standards, and many sit on rural routes with light truck traffic. Newer concrete and gentler loads could have produced the same difference, so the sealant's role remains unestablished.
choices: The sealant was the main reason the sealed decks developed less cracking.
The sealant does nothing to slow the deterioration of concrete decks.
Sealed decks in the survey cracked less than untreated decks did.
Decks built before 2005 should be replaced rather than sealed.
explanation: Text 1 reports that sealed decks showed about half as much cracking, and Text 2 opens by accepting those counts ('not in question') before disputing the cause. The two authors agree on the observation, and they split only over the explanation for it.

A.why: You picked Text 1's conclusion. Text 2 says newer concrete and lighter traffic could explain the difference, and it calls the sealant's role 'unestablished,' so the author of Text 2 would not accept this.

B.why: You read Text 2 as proving the sealant useless. Text 2 argues only that the survey doesn't show the sealant works. That is a claim about missing evidence, not proof that the sealant has no effect, and Text 1 plainly rejects it.

D.why: You latched onto the 2005 date in Text 2. Neither author makes any recommendation about replacing older decks.

rated_why: Finding agreed fact (crack counts) among contested claims requires tracking disagreement and isolating one non-disputed point

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Fossil leaves from a 56-million-year-old site in Wyoming bear unusually many insect feeding scars. Because the site dates to a brief interval of rapid global warming, paleobotanist Lena Ortiz argues that higher temperatures drove a surge in insect herbivory.

Text 2
Ortiz's damage tallies are careful, and the warm interval is well dated. But most of her leaves come from a single ancient riverbank, where fast-growing, thin-leaved plants dominated. Such plants are eaten heavily in any climate, so the scars may reflect which species happened to fossilize there rather than the warming itself.
choices: The Wyoming leaves show an unusually high level of insect feeding damage.
Rising temperatures caused the increase in insect feeding at the Wyoming site.
Temperature has no effect on how heavily insects feed on plants.
The Wyoming site is too poorly dated to be linked to the warming.
explanation: Text 1 reports unusually many feeding scars, and Text 2 calls Ortiz's damage tallies 'careful.' Both accept how much damage there is. Text 2 disputes only whether warming caused it.

B.why: This is Ortiz's conclusion, and it is the claim Text 2 is written to reject. Text 2 says the scars may reflect which plant species fossilized at the site rather than the warming.

C.why: You made Text 2 stronger than it is. Text 2 says the damage at this site may have another explanation. It never claims that temperature has no effect on herbivory in general.

D.why: Text 2 explicitly grants that 'the warm interval is well dated,' so neither author questions the site's age.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Both texts accept the damage counts as real; straightforward factual agreement despite causal disagreement

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Manuscript copies of a set of 1720s violin sonatas carry performers' pencil markings that lengthen certain notes. Musicologist Dara Feld concludes that musicians of the period routinely played uneven rhythms even where the notation was even, and that modern performers should do the same.

Text 2
The markings Feld catalogued are real and revealing. Yet nearly all appear in copies owned by a single court orchestra in Dresden, whose director was known for his idiosyncratic taste. What one ensemble did is not necessarily what musicians across Europe did.
choices: Musicians across Europe routinely played uneven rhythms in this period.
Performers outside Dresden played these sonatas exactly as written.
Modern performers should play these sonatas with strictly even rhythms.
The pencil markings show that some performers lengthened certain notes.
explanation: Text 2 calls the markings 'real and revealing,' so it accepts that at least the Dresden players lengthened notes. It does not accept that this practice was routine everywhere. Both authors agree that some performers lengthened notes, and they disagree about how widespread the practice was.

A.why: This is Feld's broad conclusion, and it is the claim Text 2 narrows. Text 2 argues that one ensemble's habits don't show what musicians across Europe did.

B.why: You treated 'not shown' as 'shown false.' Text 2 says only that the Dresden evidence can't speak for other musicians. It offers no evidence about how anyone outside Dresden played.

C.why: Text 1 recommends that modern performers use uneven rhythms, and Text 2 says nothing about modern performance. You aimed Text 2's doubt at a part of Text 1 it never addresses.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Both texts confirm the pencil markings exist; students must rule out overgeneralizations about European practice or modern performance

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
On test plots in Iowa, fields planted with a winter rye cover crop yielded 8 percent more soybeans the following summer than fields left bare. Agronomist Priya Nair concluded that rye cover crops raise soybean yields and urged farmers across the Midwest to adopt them.

Text 2
Nair's plots did produce more soybeans. That trial, however, ran during two unusually dry summers, when rye's mulch helps soil hold moisture. In wetter years, other trials have found that rye can delay spring soil warming and slightly reduce yields, so the benefit may hold only under drought.
choices: Rye cover crops raise soybean yields in Midwest fields in most years.
Rye plots in Nair's dry-summer trial yielded more soybeans than bare plots.
Rye cover crops lower soybean yields in all but the driest years.
Soil temperature matters more to soybeans than soil moisture does.
explanation: Text 2 grants the result directly: 'Nair's plots did produce more soybeans.' Where it parts from Text 1 is scope, since the gain may hold only in drought years like those of the trial. Both authors therefore accept the trial's result.

A.why: This is Nair's general conclusion. Text 2 limits it by saying the benefit may appear only in dry years, so it would not grant that rye helps in most years.

C.why: You turned Text 2's hedges ('can,' 'slightly,' 'may') into a firm rule. Text 1 would reject this claim in any case, because Nair found that rye raised yields.

D.why: Text 2 mentions both soil temperature and soil moisture, but neither author ranks one above the other.

rated_why: Both accept Nair's plot results; requires identifying the single factual claim uncontested despite disagreement over generalization

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After a city installed reflective white roofing on 3,000 buildings, summer afternoon temperatures downtown averaged 0.9°C lower than in the previous five summers. The city's climate office concluded that the roofing program had cooled the downtown area.

Text 2
Downtown was indeed cooler over that period. But the same summers were cooler across the entire region, including rural stations far from any new roofs, because of a persistent shift in the jet stream. Unless the downtown drop exceeded the regional one, the roofs cannot be credited with it.
choices: The reflective roofing was responsible for the cooler downtown afternoons.
Reflective roofing does not lower temperatures in city centers.
The regional cooling was confined to areas near the new roofs.
Downtown summer afternoons were cooler after the roofing program began.
explanation: Text 2 opens with 'Downtown was indeed cooler,' which accepts the temperature drop that Text 1 reports. Text 2 then offers a different cause, a regional jet-stream shift. The cooling itself is the common ground.

A.why: This is the climate office's conclusion, and Text 2 rejects it. Text 2 says the roofs can't be credited unless downtown cooled more than the region as a whole.

B.why: You picked the 'proves the opposite' version. Text 2 says only that this record doesn't show the roofs worked. It makes no general claim that reflective roofs can't cool cities.

C.why: Text 2 says the cooling reached 'rural stations far from any new roofs,' which is the opposite of this statement.

rated_why: Both confirm downtown cooled; finding this shared fact requires separating the measurement from its interpretation

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Banding records show that American robins in a Minnesota study area now arrive in spring about twelve days earlier than they did in 1980. Ornithologist Sam Okafor concludes that the birds have evolved to migrate earlier in response to warming winters.

Text 2
Okafor's arrival dates are solid. His explanation, though, is premature. Robins adjust their pace to the weather they meet along the way, and an individual bird can shift its timing from one year to the next. Earlier arrivals may therefore reflect flexible behavior rather than any inherited change.
choices: The robins' earlier arrival reflects an inherited change in timing.
Robins now reach the study area earlier in spring than in 1980.
Warming winters have had no influence on when the robins arrive.
An individual robin keeps the same migration schedule from year to year.
explanation: Text 2 calls Okafor's arrival dates 'solid' and calls only his explanation 'premature.' Both authors accept that the robins arrive earlier. They disagree over whether evolution or flexible behavior explains it.

A.why: This is Okafor's evolutionary conclusion, which Text 2 calls premature because flexible behavior could explain the same arrival dates.

C.why: You made Text 2 deny any role for climate. Text 2 actually says robins respond to the weather they meet, so it never claims warming has no influence, and Text 1 would reject this statement outright.

D.why: Text 2 states that an individual bird 'can shift its timing from one year to the next,' so this reverses what Text 2 says.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: distinguishes fact (earlier arrival) from disputed explanation (evolution)

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Divers surveying a Caribbean reef counted 40 percent more juvenile parrotfish inside a newly protected zone than in fished waters nearby, just three years after fishing was banned there. The researchers concluded that the ban had allowed the parrotfish population to rebound.

Text 2
The survey found more juveniles inside the zone—that much is clear. Yet the zone was drawn around the reef's densest seagrass beds, which parrotfish larvae favor when they settle. The zone may simply have held more juveniles all along; without counts from before the ban, a rebound has not been shown.
choices: More juvenile parrotfish were counted inside the zone than outside it.
The fishing ban allowed the zone's parrotfish population to rebound.
The fishing ban has done nothing to help the reef's parrotfish.
Parrotfish larvae tend to avoid seagrass beds when they settle.
explanation: Text 2 grants the survey result ('that much is clear') and then argues that the difference may have existed before the ban. Both authors accept the higher count inside the zone.

B.why: This is Text 1's conclusion. Text 2 says that without counts from before the ban, a rebound 'has not been shown.'

C.why: You mistook 'not shown' for 'disproved.' Text 2 says the evidence is missing. It never says the ban failed.

D.why: Text 2 says larvae favor seagrass beds when they settle, which is the reverse of this statement.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
A 1507 world map held in a private archive shows a narrow strait at the southern tip of South America, thirteen years before Magellan's crew sailed through one. Historian Elise Marrow argues that the mapmaker must have drawn on reports from an earlier, unrecorded voyage to the region.

Text 2
Marrow is right that the strait appears on the map, and the map's date is secure. Mapmakers of the era, however, often drew speculative channels where they believed one ought to exist, since a westward passage was eagerly sought. The strait could be a lucky guess rather than a record of anyone's voyage.
choices: The mapmaker drew on reports from an earlier voyage to the region.
The map was most likely drawn after Magellan's voyage.
The 1507 map shows a strait at South America's southern tip.
No European ship reached the region before Magellan's crew did.
explanation: Text 2 states that 'Marrow is right that the strait appears on the map.' Both authors accept what the map shows. Text 2 disputes only Marrow's claim that the strait records a real voyage.

A.why: This is Marrow's conclusion. Text 2 suggests the strait could be a speculative guess, so it would not agree.

B.why: Text 2 grants that 'the map's date is secure,' so neither author doubts that the map predates Magellan.

D.why: You read Text 2 as ruling out an earlier voyage. Text 2 says only that the map doesn't prove one happened. It makes no claim that no such voyage took place.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After beavers were reintroduced along a tributary of Oregon's John Day River, hydrologists recorded a 20 percent rise in late-summer streamflow below the new dams over five years. The dams, they reasoned, slow spring runoff and push water into the surrounding soil, which releases it gradually during dry months. They therefore concluded that the beaver dams caused the higher summer flows.

Text 2
The increase in summer flow on the tributary is not in question. However, the five study years coincided with unusually deep winter snowpack in the region, and heavier snowmelt alone could have produced the same rise. Until that effect is accounted for, crediting the dams is premature.
choices: Late-summer streamflow below the dams increased during the period that was studied.
The beaver dams were responsible for the increase in late-summer streamflow.
The deep winter snowpack was the sole cause of the rise in late-summer streamflow.
Reintroducing beavers is an unreliable way to manage water in dry regions.
explanation: Write the two sentences first. Author 1 thinks the dams raised summer flow. Author 2 thinks the rise is real but could be explained by snowmelt. Text 2 opens by granting the observation ('is not in question') and then disputes only the explanation. The point they share is the observation itself: summer flow went up during the study.

B.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and Text 2 was written to push back on it. Author 2 calls crediting the dams 'premature,' so you picked the one claim the authors actually disagree on.

C.why: Author 2 says only that snowmelt 'could have' caused the rise, which means the dams have not been proven to be the cause. This choice turns that doubt into a firm claim of the opposite. Even Author 2 does not go that far, and Author 1 would reject it.

D.why: Neither text judges beaver reintroduction as a water-management policy. The texts argue about what caused one measured rise in flow, and this choice moves to a broader question that neither author takes up.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Over three years, astronomers watched the star HD 41870 dim irregularly, sometimes losing nearly a fifth of its brightness for weeks at a time. No orbiting planet could block that much light. The team concluded that a vast cloud of debris, left by a collision between two young planets, is passing in front of the star.

Text 2
The star's dimming episodes are certainly real, and they are unusually deep. But dust warmed by a star glows in infrared light, and follow-up infrared surveys of HD 41870 found no such excess. A collision debris cloud therefore seems an unlikely cause. Changes within the star itself deserve closer study.
choices: A debris cloud left by colliding planets is blocking part of the star's light.
The star's dimming is too slight to be measured with any confidence.
HD 41870 has dimmed irregularly by large amounts over the period observed.
Changes within HD 41870 have been shown to cause its dimming episodes.
explanation: Author 1 thinks a debris cloud from a planetary collision is dimming the star. Author 2 thinks the dimming is real but that missing infrared glow makes a debris cloud unlikely. Text 2 begins with 'certainly real' and then turns with 'But,' which shows you what the authors share: the star really has dimmed, deeply and irregularly.

A.why: This is the conclusion Text 1 ends on, and Text 2 calls it 'unlikely.' Picking it means you agreed with the very claim Author 2 is rejecting.

B.why: Both authors describe the dimming as large. Text 1 reports losses of nearly a fifth of the star's brightness, and Text 2 calls the episodes 'unusually deep.' This choice reverses what both texts say.

D.why: Author 2 says only that changes within the star 'deserve closer study,' which suggests a possibility and does not claim proof. This choice treats that suggestion as an established result, and Author 1 would not accept it anyway.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Paleobotanists examined thousands of fossil leaves from Wyoming dating to a sharp warming event 56 million years ago. Leaves from the warmest interval showed far more insect chewing and boring than leaves from before it. Because insects grow and feed faster in heat, the researchers concluded that the warming increased insect damage to plants across the globe.

Text 2
Although the Wyoming leaves clearly record a rise in insect damage, fossil floras from Patagonia spanning the same warming event show no such increase. Local factors such as rainfall or the mix of plant species may have mattered as much as temperature. The global claim reaches beyond the evidence.
choices: The warming event increased insect damage to plants in every region of the globe.
Fossil leaves from Wyoming show more insect damage during the warmest interval.
The warming event reduced insect damage to plants at most fossil sites worldwide.
Fossil leaves from Patagonia are better preserved than those found in Wyoming.
explanation: Author 1 thinks the warming raised insect damage worldwide. Author 2 thinks the Wyoming rise is real but that Patagonia shows it did not happen everywhere. Text 2 narrows the claim without denying the finding: it opens with 'Although the Wyoming leaves clearly record a rise.' The point the authors share is that Wyoming finding.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion, and Text 2 says it 'reaches beyond the evidence.' You picked the global claim that the Patagonia fossils were brought in to limit.

C.why: Author 2 reports one region with no increase. That does not show a decrease, and it says nothing about most sites. This choice turns a narrowed claim into a claim of the opposite, which neither author makes.

D.why: Neither text compares how well the fossils from the two regions are preserved. The Patagonia floras matter only because of what they show about insect damage, so this choice focuses on a detail the texts never raise.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Comparing eighteenth-century charts of the Adriatic coast, historian Ines Vardaro found that harbors on charts made by naval surveyors were misplaced by only about one-third as much as harbors on charts sold by commercial engravers. Vardaro concluded that the naval surveyors' superior instruments explain the gap.

Text 2
The naval charts are certainly more accurate, but crediting their instruments is premature. Naval surveyors often spent months at a single harbor, whereas engravers usually copied older charts without visiting the coast at all. Time spent on site could have produced the same difference.
choices: Harbors on the naval surveyors' charts were placed more accurately than harbors on the engravers' charts.
The naval surveyors' instruments account for most of the gap in accuracy between the two kinds of charts.
The naval surveyors' instruments were no more precise than the tools the commercial engravers used.
Time spent at each harbor is the likeliest explanation for the gap in accuracy between the charts.
explanation: Start with the two sentences. Author 1 thinks the naval charts were more accurate *because of better instruments*. Author 2 thinks they were more accurate, but that the instruments haven't been shown to be the reason. Text 2 grants the observation ("The naval charts are certainly more accurate") and rejects only the explanation. The ground they share is the observed gap itself: the naval charts placed harbors more accurately.

B.why: This is Vardaro's conclusion, and it is the exact claim Text 2 calls "premature." You picked the one statement the second author refuses to accept.

C.why: Text 2 only says the instruments haven't been shown to be the cause. It never claims they were no better. You read "not established" as "proven false," which is stronger than anything Text 2 says.

D.why: Only Text 2 offers time on site, and only as a possibility ("could have"). Vardaro credits instruments instead. The question asks for something both authors hold, and this is one author's alternative.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Hydrologist Tomas Brekke monitored twelve forested basins for six years after half of them were thinned. By late summer, streams in the thinned basins carried roughly twice as much water as streams in the untouched ones. Brekke therefore concluded that thinning raises late-summer streamflow throughout the region's watersheds.

Text 2
Although Brekke's measurements are sound, his conclusion reaches too far. Many of the region's basins sit on porous volcanic rock, where water that trees no longer use sinks into deep aquifers rather than feeding streams. In those basins, thinning is unlikely to raise summer flow.
choices: In Brekke's study, thinned basins had greater late-summer streamflow than basins left untouched.
Thinning raises late-summer streamflow in watersheds across the entire region Brekke studied.
Thinning reduces late-summer streamflow in basins that sit on porous volcanic rock.
Deep aquifers supply most of the late-summer streamflow in the region's watersheds.
explanation: Author 1 thinks thinning raised summer flow in the study basins, so it must do so across the region. Author 2 accepts the measurements ("Brekke's measurements are sound") but says the regional conclusion "reaches too far" because porous-rock basins behave differently. Text 2 narrows the claim without disputing the data, so both authors accept the measured gap: thinned basins carried more late-summer water than untouched ones.

B.why: This is Brekke's final conclusion, the sentence Text 2 was written to answer. Text 2 says it doesn't hold for basins on porous rock, so the second author would reject it.

C.why: Text 2 says thinning is "unlikely to raise" flow in those basins. It doesn't say thinning lowers it. You turned "no increase" into "a decrease," which claims more than the text supports.

D.why: Aquifers come up in Text 2 only to explain where water goes on porous rock. Neither author says aquifers supply most streamflow. You took a side detail from one text and made it a shared claim.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Art historian Mireille Contat examined woodblock prints from a Lyon workshop active in the 1840s. Impressions pulled late in a print run showed color only about half as saturated as impressions pulled early. Contat concluded that the workshop's printers deliberately thinned their pigments as runs went on to save money.

Text 2
The late impressions are undeniably paler, but Contat's inference of thrift is difficult to accept. Cherry blocks swell with moisture and their surfaces wear during long runs. An unchanged pigment mixture could simply have transferred less color as the block aged.
choices: Impressions pulled late in the workshop's print runs are paler than those pulled early.
The workshop's printers deliberately thinned their pigments to lower the cost of long runs.
The workshop's printers never altered their pigment mixtures in the course of a print run.
Swelling and wear of cherry blocks mattered more than pigment cost in the workshop's runs.
explanation: Author 1 thinks late prints are paler because printers thinned pigment to save money. Author 2 thinks late prints are paler, but block swelling and wear could explain it just as well. This is the same observation with a different explanation: Text 2 grants that the late impressions are "undeniably paler" and disputes only the cause. The paleness itself is what both authors accept.

B.why: This is Contat's conclusion, the one Text 2 calls "difficult to accept." You picked the claim under attack instead of the observation both texts share.

C.why: Text 2 only offers a way the paleness could have happened without thinning ("could simply have"). It never claims the printers kept the mixture unchanged. You read doubt about Contat's claim as proof of its opposite.

D.why: Block swelling and wear appear only in Text 2, as a possible mechanism. Contat never weighs them against cost. This states one author's alternative, not a view the two authors share.
